title: How Racial Resentment Relates to Political Conservatism Across Different White Religious
author: Eric W. Dolan
summary: Sociologist Philip Schwadel, analyzing General Social Survey data from 8,048 White Americans collected between 2002 and 2022, finds that racial resentment functions very differently as a predictor of political conservatism depending on religious tradition. Among White evangelical Protestants, conservatism is near-universal regardless of racial attitudes—a ceiling effect—because evangelicals are already politically conservative. But among White mainline Protestants, Catholics, non-Christian religious affiliates, and the unaffiliated, racial resentment is a powerful predictor of conservatism: those with high racial resentment in these groups look politically indistinguishable from evangelicals. The study does not exculpate evangelicals—they remain significantly more likely to hold racially resentful views than non-evangelicals—but the finding reframes the conversation: racial resentment is not primarily an evangelical phenomenon but a broad organizing force that shapes conservatism across many religious contexts. This has significant implications for catechesis, civic formation, and pastoral leadership.
points: Understand the ceiling effect: racial resentment doesn't differentiate political beliefs among White evangelicals because they are already near-uniformly conservative; this means racial formation work in evangelical contexts must operate on different leverage points than in mainline or Catholic contexts.

Recognize that racial resentment functions as a quasi-religious political commitment across many religious traditions—not just evangelical ones—and pastoral and civic leadership must address it directly rather than assuming it is someone else's problem.

Use the study's finding to resist the temptation to isolate racial resentment as an evangelical problem: White mainline Protestants, Catholics, and the unaffiliated with high racial resentment are politically indistinguishable from evangelicals.

Distinguish racial resentment (symbolic racism—the belief that Black Americans should overcome disadvantages without assistance) from explicit prejudice; this form of belief is often held by people who would not describe themselves as prejudiced.

Commit to longitudinal research and formation strategies that track how religious identity, racial attitudes, and political alignment shift together over time, rather than drawing static conclusions from cross-sectional data.
quotes: Racial resentment cannot explain differences in the likelihood of being politically conservative among white evangelicals because they are almost all politically conservative.

Non-evangelical white Americans, on the other hand, are not particularly likely to be politically conservative. But, non-evangelical whites with higher levels of racial resentment are far more likely to be politically conservative than non-evangelical whites with lower levels of racial resentment.
Among those with high levels of racial resentment, there is little to no difference in the likelihood of being politically conservative between white evangelical and non-evangelical Americans.

I want to be clear that white evangelicals are considerably more likely than white non-evangelicals to express racial resentment. It is just that racial resentment doesn't explain political differences among white evangelicals like it does among other white Americans.

The research and popular discourse on racism/racial resentment, religion, and politics focuses on how views of race connect white evangelical Christians to conservative politics and the Republican party.
